answer:
My assessment: the selection choices fit the experiment’s stated boundary, but I would correct the procedure omission and the visible mid-scroll qualification failure before the PO demonstration. The latter is a factual presentation problem, not merely unattractive wrapping. Nothing here warrants removing the connected timeline.

I reviewed the pasted artifacts, not their on-disk originals. I also recovered the September 9, 2026 predecessor consultation at @session:default/run_5c2d0e03ac8448588e75529e8eda5895. Its recommendations were design advice, not PO acceptance. I take the adopted boundary and newer PO feedback from your supplied account; I have not independently verified the current project authority.

Selection is appropriate. Case A supplies chronology, with approximate time and observational sources distinguished. Case C supplies a mandatory action order, not execution history. Case B supplies competing alternatives whose price ordering is not a procedural or temporal relationship; choosing prose avoids suggesting that the organizer should progress through suppliers. That supports these particular choices. The author’s individual audience/choice explanations for A/C are not among the pasted artifacts, so I cannot assess the full reported reasoning.

Case A is substantively faithful. In case-a-final.json, the labels retain “sensor reported” and “Approximately 18:25 — Technician note reported,” rather than converting reports into an independently established roof state or an exact timestamp. The scope preserves the date, local times and incomplete selection. The notes retain unknown adjustment, cause and camera restoration, and deny any supplied current state or safety clearance. Both supplied A captures show those qualifications. “Chronology / supplied event order / not causation” is helpful; the connected gutter is not itself evidence of a causal claim. I find no material factual correction in A.

Case C omits an operative instruction. The prompt says “assign the batch identifier from the intake sheet”; case-c-final.json’s first label says only “Assign the batch identifier,” and its detail never restores the source. This leaves room to invent an identifier rather than obtain it from the specified sheet. It also makes the later “same intake sheet” less well anchored. Restore “from the intake sheet,” preferably in the first label. This is a procedural fidelity correction, particularly because the persistent scope promises the “Complete supplied intake procedure.”

Case C also exposes a material scrolling failure. In case-c-80x24-end.txt, the first visible item text is “01 │ actual identifier is supplied for this fictional example.” In the complete paragraph, that text is preceded by “no,” on the previous, now-hidden line. The viewport therefore presents an affirmative fragment where the supplied fact is negative. Re-identifying item 01 preserves ownership, not meaning. This is evidence that numbered continuation alone does not protect qualifications. My recommendation is to prevent this particular misleading fragment before demonstration and check reachable scroll boundaries for equivalent losses of negation, attribution and prerequisites. That does not prescribe a connector-removal pass or a general resolver.

C otherwise handles the central permission boundary well. The final label begins “Only after donor permission is recorded,” keeping the prerequisite with the action; its detail says permission is not established. The persistent provenance says “not executed,” and the relationship explicitly disclaims execution status. At 80x24 the notes about unknowns and the procedure ending before scanning require scrolling, but “MORE below” announces that, and the supplied end capture exposes them. Scrolling itself is a presentation cost, not an omission. However, the evidence does not establish that the permission qualifier remains intelligible at every intermediate offset.

Case B needs smaller fidelity corrections. In case-b-final.txt, replace “$40,” “$55” and “$70” with explicit USD: the prompt specifies currency, while “$” alone does not. Also retain that these are fictional supplied facts, not live or independently verified quotes; “supplied quote comparison” preserves attribution but not fictional status when the file is read alone. These are specificity/provenance losses, not invented prices or a fabricated winner. By contrast, “The numbers below” introducing unnumbered bullets is merely an editorial mismatch. The price order remains intact; “Listed in ascending quoted price, not preference” would suffice. Cedar’s unknown delivered total is correctly adjacent to its offer, and no unsupported supplier recommendation or calendar date is introduced.

The trial demonstrates that these supplied final compositions can communicate the intended relationship choices, with substantial qualification retention at the shown sizes. It also demonstrates a concrete limitation: persistent global context and item identity do not guarantee locally faithful text at scroll boundaries.

It does not establish implementation correctness, the reported 67-test result, frozen-hash integrity, complete offset coverage, actual terminal styling or interaction quality, reproducible author independence, general author success rates, or PO/production acceptance. The discovery entrypoint, drafts, author report, clamped-offset outputs, terminal excerpt and reconstructed error file were described but not pasted here. I cannot audit them; reconstructed stderr would not establish the original diagnostic anyway. The reported unaided repair is encouraging evidence about one authoring attempt, not proof of low effort or broad discoverability.

For the demonstration, my judgment is to present this as a bounded experiment with identified corrections and remaining viewport limitations—not as a completed validation. Whether the resulting readability and scrolling cost are acceptable remains a PO judgment; these artifacts do not supply that acceptance.
note: Dottie evidence/context, not implementation authorization. No automatic retry.
